title: Contribute
text:
Clone the repository, add a protocol in markdown format and push it. The website is built automatically after every push. The link to the github repo is github.com/kpc002/protocols-website. Currently this repository is private, so message me if you want access.
If you see a mistake, you can modify the current site my clicking on Edit this page on the right side of each site.
The website is generated using quarto. See their website to learn more about the structure of the webpage.

title: Cage Card Stickers
text:
Cage Card Stickers

Can only use the computer down in the vivarium. There’s usually only one computer in the vivarium that is used to print cage card stickers. This computer is usually set up on a cart along the hallway.
The computer is already set up with the program/page for printing stickers with 2 number fields. One for code and one for number of stickers to be printed.

Enter the code for each vivarium. Need to use the code designated for each vivarium, Pac Hall code will not work on NSB computer and vice versa.

NSB code: 232512-1
Pac Hall: 243322-1

Enter the desired number of stickers to be printed. The bigger the number, the longer it will take to print.

NSB vivarium tech will usually bring the stickers back into the mouse room but Pac hall tech will not.


Bring the stickers back into the mouse room after it’s done printing.

title: Duties of the Radiation S
text:
Duties of the Radiation Safety Officer:
Monthly Surveys:
These are the most important. A survey must be done each calendar month for both our lab (when chromium or tritium is present) and the shared radioactive bay. Missing a month will lead to a ding on our safety report!
32P – this can be detected using a Geiger counter with the ‘pancake’ probe. The half life is 2 weeks.
51Cr – also can be detected using a Geiger counter with the ‘pancake’ probe. The half life is 3 weeks.
3H – This can only be detected using a swipe test. The half life is a very long time…
To survey our lab:
Use the Geiger counter for the 51-Cr area. If no Cr was used/ordered that month you can skip the survey and just fill in “no Cr for month of ___” on the survey sheet.
Swipe tests for 3H should be done in all places where the 3H is used or stored. This often includes the Tissue culture hoods and the –20C freezer in TC. Make sure to swipe something that 3H should never have come in contact with to see what your background is.
Monthly survey of the shared space:
This involves carefully using the Geiger counter to go over all benches, sinks, etc. of the shared radioactive area, as well as any other rooms (they are listed on the left-hand side of the survey sheet) where radioactivity is used.
These duties are shared between our lab and the T. Johnson, R. Johnson and Niwa labs, which means this is only done 3X per year by us. As of 05/07, Herve from the T. Johnson lab is coordinating these surveys. When it is our lab’s turn to complete the survey, make copies for the other labs and leave them on the wall outside our TC room. Make sure to have a copy from each month so that our safety binder is complete!
Swipe Test:
Simply cut up filter paper into ~ 1”x1” squares. Wipe it over the surface of any areas to be tested and put it into a scintillation vial. Add scintillation fluid until the paper is wet/mostly covered. Take it to the scintillation counter and count.
Using the Scintillation Counter:
The scintillation vials to put your samples in are located in the cabinet to the left of the sink in the shared area. Additional vials may be purchased from the chemical storehouse under Urey Hall.
When you have your samples ready, hit ‘main menu’ and select ‘count single rack’. Then hit ‘select user program’. Choose program 1 for swipe tests or program 5 for 32P. Put your samples into a white rack hit ‘select’ then ‘start’. Program 1 counts for 5 min/sample and program 5 for 1 min/sample, so plan your return time accordingly.
Geiger Counter Maintenance:
The meter must be taken in annually to be calibrated. Take it to the radioactivity pick-up location (see below) and EH&S will take care of it. This is where our meter should also go if it needs to be serviced.
Waste Pickup:
All waster should be kept separate ( i.e. 51 Cr waste does not belong with 32 P waste). Also, dry waste is separate from liquid etc. Once a bag/carboy of waste is started, it should have a tag on it complete with our waste generator number, the name of a contact person responsible for the waste, and what is inside. Pick-ups are done by EH&S first thing on Tuesday and Thursday mornings.
The URL for the waste pickup is:
http://www-ehs.ucsd.edu/hazwaste/cgi-forms/collection_request.html
The other way to get to the waste pick-up form is to go to http://blink.ucsd.edu and go to the safety section. Under radioactive safety choose “waste”. In this section directions are given regarding collection of hazardous waste. To schedule a pickup, click on the link to request a hazardous waste collection. Fill out and submit the form!
Once you have submitted the form, double check that dry waste and source vials are double-bagged and sealed off and that the lid is on the liquid waste. Make sure all waste is fully labeled ( you can estimate the amount of waste to be picked up. Something around 1 mCi is generally a good estimate).
Radioactivity Ordering and Pick-up:
To order radioactivity it is generally best to call in the order yourself (although if you enter it into the database then Andrea will order it, but it will take an extra day). See the order database for important numbers, etc.
Currently the EH&S services lab delivers our radioactivity, but it usually doesn’t come until late in the day. If you need it sooner, then it can be picked up at the EH&S services lab at the address below.
Important Contact Info:
• EH&S Services Lab, University Center 301-B
- Mail Code: 0035
- Phone: (858) 534-6418
- Fax: (858) 822-5524
• Hazardous Materials Spill
- Environment, Health & Safety:

534-3660   weekdays, 8 a.m. – 4:30 p.m.


- Campus Police:

534-4357 evenings and weekends


The radioactivity section on Blink is full of good information regarding all aspects of use. I would strongly recommend any frequent user to look through it.

title: -80 Freezer Maintenance
text:
-80 Freezer (Revco UXF) – Thermofisher
Serial Number: 0132864801140430
Model Number: UXF50086A
Item Number: 152AR5A01A
Service Team: AGR Mechanical
619-977-0271
agrmechanicalsd@gamil.com
Maintenance for the -80:

Must be defrosted at minimum once a year
The middle of the freezer must always be full
If freezer is not completely full, fill it with empty shelves
Clean the filter in the front every month

Slide out the metal guard
Slide out the filter
Wash with warm water and dry overnight
Replace filter and guard next morning

Clean the filter on the bottom every month

Slide out the 2inch filter under the front side of the freezer
Wash with warm water and dry
Replace the filter that same day

Shave off ice once a month
Clean the compressors and system on the side of the -80 annually

AGR will do this as part of their service

If it is not maintaining temperature or losing temperature quickly, call AGR Mechanical

They come out the same day or next day and will monitor the machine and give a diagnostics report

Service the machine regularly

AGR has a service where they come out and clean the machine, check the system, monitor it for an hour, and regulate the compressors, etc
$135/service or $290/4 services in one year


*Note: Apparently our system, is the “older” version of this machine and has lower watts than the newer models, which is why it takes a little longer to get back to the correct temperature, but as told by the technician, this is expected with this model.
Last serviced by AGR Mechanical: March 16, 2021 (CT)

title: Allen Institute Mouse order
text:
AHR 249 BSL2 Procedures/Workflow:
Things to note:

Isofluorane must be checked out from 4th floor cabinet and cannot be left unattended at any point
You MUST change into scrubs before entering BSL2 and after exiting BSL2, must change into clean clothes before re-entering lab spaces (ie you take iso down to locker room with you)
My normal flow:

Drop of cooler outside AHR 249
Go downstairs and change into scrubs
Go up to 4th floor drug cabinet
Check out isofluorane
Go to 249 AHR – put on appropriate PPE over scrubs
After procedure/collecting samples: Leave cooler outside 249 near elevator (take iso with you to locker room)
Change back into clothes
Back up to 4th floor to check iso back in (record amount used)
Back to 2nd floor to retrieve cooler
Back to 220 for processing

ALL LCMV or INFECTIOUS experiments MUST be carried out in a BSC (even after clearance timepoint), if propagating or making stocks must also wear mask

title: CB1.Thawing Frozen Cells
text:
Protocol for Thawing Frozen Cells
(modified from https://www.thermofisher.com/it/en/home/references/gibco-cell-culture-basics/cell-culture-protocols/thawing-cells.html)
The thawing procedure is stressful to frozen cells, and using good technique and working quickly ensures that a high proportion of the cells survive the procedure.  As with other cell culture procedures, we recommend that you closely follow the instructions provided with your cells and other reagents for best results.
NOTE:

Thaw frozen cells rapidly (< 1 minute) in a 37°C water bath.
Dilute the thawed cells slowly, using pre-warmed growth medium.
Plate thawed cells at high density to optimize recovery.
Always use proper aseptic technique and work in a laminar flow hood.
Always wear personal protective equipment, including a face mask or goggles.  Cryovials stored in liquid-phase present a risk of explosion when thawed.
Some freezing media contain DMSO, which is known to facilitate the entry of organic molecules into tissues. Handle reagents containing DMSO using equipment

Materials

Cryovial containing frozen cells
Complete growth medium, pre-warmed to 37°C
Disposable, sterile centrifuge tubes
Water bath at 37°C
70% ethanol

Protocol
The following protocol describes a general procedure for thawing cryopreserved cells.  For detailed protocols, always refer to the cell-specific product insert.

Remove the cryovial containing the frozen cells from liquid nitrogen storage and immediately place it into a 37°C water bath.
Quickly thaw the cells (< 1 minute) by gently swirling the vial in the 37°C water bath until there is just a small bit of ice left in the vial.
Transfer the vial into a laminar flow hood.  Before opening, wipe the outside of the vial with 70% ethanol.
Add 1mL pre-warmed complete growth medium dropwise into the cryovial containing frozen cells.
Gently resuspend the cells in complete growth medium, and transfer them into a Conical Centrifuge Tube (Falcon™ 15mL or 50mL Conical Centrifuge Tubes) with the desired amount of pre-warmed complete growth medium appropriate for the number of your cells (e.g. 10mL for up to 107 cells, 20mL for up to 5x107 cells).
Centrifuge the cell suspension at approximately 400 × g for 6 minutes.  The actual centrifugation speed and duration varies depending on the cell type.
After the centrifugation, check the clarity of supernatant and visibility of a complete pellet. Aseptically decant the supernatant without disturbing the cell pellet.
Gently resuspend the cells with complete growth medium or with the buffer of interest.

ADDITIONAL NOTE

If you are going to perform viability staining with Live Dead from Invitrogen or with Zombie Fixable Viability Kit from BioLegend, resuspend cells with PBS without calcium and magnesium in order to remove residual of Fetal Bovine Serum (FBS) or Fetal Calf Serum (FCS) contained in the complete growth medium used for thawing procedure.
If you have high content of dead cells, you can use DNase I for removing dead cells’ DNA during sample preparation. We add DNase both to the complete growth medium used for thawing cells, both to the PBS used for washing cells after thawing. We use “Deoxyribonuclease I from bovine pancreas” from SIGMA ALDRICH DN25 (stock 5mg/mL, final concentration: 20 ug/mL).

title: Human tumor sample collection, processing, and flow analysis
text:
TUMOR TISSUE PROCESSING
Sample ID:________ Patient ID:________
Collection Date/Time:________ Processing Date/Time:________
Processing Scientist Initials:_______
SAMPLE PREPARATION

Ideally at least one week prior to collection, identify samples and ensure sufficient amounts of antibody. Book flow time on cytometer for the day of processing
Day before or day of tissue collection, prepare 50mL conical tube with 25mL RPMI/10%FBS/1% Pen-Strep. If multiple samples, prepare multiple tubes (for both collection, as well as processing and flow steps below)
Record mass of tissue at time of collection, and record




POST-COLLECTION MASS OF TUBE (g): _______________


MASS OF FLOW TISSUE (g):_______________


SAMPLE PROCESSING

Prepare enzymatic processing tube: 50mL conical containing 4.7mL RPMI-1640 (no FBS/Pen-Strep, or L-Glut) + 200 µL Enzyme H + 100 µL Enzyme R + 25 µL Enzyme A (Tumor Dissociation Kit from Miltenyi).
Remove tissue from 50mL collection conical tube and place into petri dish, and dissect into small pieces using scalpel or sterile scissors. Transfer sample into gentleMACS “C Tube” using the enzymatic solution, making sure to transfer all tissue.
Tightly close tube, attach it upside down into one of the two sleeves on the gentleMACS dissociator (either sleeve may be used). Make sure tumor samples are near the rotor/stator and not adhered to the upper walls of the tube. Ensure tube is seated properly. You should hear and feel a “click” when the tube is properly attached.
Run gentleMACS program “h_tumor_01”.
Detach tube. Incubate for 30 minutes at 37ºC with continuous rotation. If tube rotator is not available, manually rotate/agitate tube every ~5 minutes.
Attach tube to gentleMACS dissociator, run program “h_tumor_01” (second time doing this).
Detach tube. Incubate for 30 minutes at 37ºC with continuous rotation. If tube rotator is not available, manually rotate/agitate tube every ~5 minutes.
Attach tube to gentleMACS dissociator, run program “h_tumor_01” (third time doing this).
Using sterile RPMI-1640, resuspend sample/wash out of C tube and cap, strain through a 70 µm filter and wash with ~20ml media.
Should have a (mostly) single cell suspension free of chunks of tissue. Centrifuge at 300xg for 5 minutes.
Resuspend sample in FACS buffer and aliquot sample to appropriate flow tubes for downstream staining. Proceed to flow staining as below.


TUMOR IMMUNE CELL ANALYSIS
Surface stain


Centrifuge samples for 5min at 300xg, and gently remove supernatant.
Resuspend samples in surface antibody solutions.
Incubate samples for 30min on ice in the dark.
Wash samples with 250μl FACS buffer, spin down 5min at 300xg, and gently remove supernatant.

Fixation, Permeabilization and Cytokine/TF staining

Resuspend cells with 100μL of eBioscience transcription factor fixation buffer per well, and incubate 30min. on ice in dark.
Prepare solution of 1x PermWash by diluting 10x PermWash to 1x in sterile H2O. Add 100μl 1x PermWash to each sample, spin down 5min at 300xg, and gently remove supernatant.
Wash cells with 100µl 1x PermWash, spin 5min. at 300xg, gently remove supernatant.
Add intracellular staining solutions as follows, and incubate 60min at room temperature in the dark.
While samples are incubating with intracellular stain, prepare individual compensation controls using eBioscience UltraComp eBeads with individual antibodies from lymphocyte panel, as well as unstained beads. Also prepare Sphero Rainbow beads (drop of positive and negative beads + 200μl FACS buffer). Rainbow beads are especially important to maintain consistency across donors and across collection timepoints.
Add 150µl 1x PermWash, spin down 5min at 300xg, gently remove supernatant.
Resuspend samples in 250μl FACS buffer, and transfer to flow tubes.
Flow samples

RUNNING AND ANALYSIS OF FLOW DATA

For all populations (lymphocyte, Treg, and myeloid), gate on singlets (FSC-A x FSC-H), cellular events (FSC-A x SSC-A), live events (Ghost Dye780 x SSC-A), dump negative events (Mouse CD8-FITC x SSC-A), and CD45+ events (CD45-PE-Cy7 x SSC-A).
After isolating CD45+ cells, go through and evaluate panels using individual analysis


LYMPHOCYTE PANEL:
CD4+ and CD8+ T cells, CD19+ B cells, NK cells (CD3- CD56+), and NK-T cells (CD3+ CD56+). We will then evaluate markers of T cell memory (CD45RO and CD26), T cell activation/exhaustion (PD-1 and TIM-3), as well as a PD-1 responsive stem-like population of CD8+ T cells (HLA-DR+ CD38+ Ki67+).
Treg PANEL:
To evaluate regulatory T cell populations, samples will be stained with CD45, CD3, CD4, CD25, GITR, CD127, and Foxp3
MYELOID PANEL:
CD45, CD11b, CD11c, CD14, CD15, CD16, CD33, CD40, CD103, HLA-DR, and will also be evaluated for expression of PD-L1.


Monocytes (CD11b+ CD11c+ CD14+ CD16lo HLA-DR+)
Macrophages (CD11b+ CD11c+ CD33+ CD14- CD16+ M1 macrophages and CD11b+ CD11c+ CD33+ CD14+ CD16+ M2 macrophages),
Dendritic cells (CD11c+ CD14+ CD16- CD103+ HLA-DR+, with CD40 expression used to identify activated DCs),
Myeloid-derived suppressor cells (CD11b+ HLA-DRlo/neg CD33+ CD14+ CD15- monocyte MDSC and CD11bb+ HLA-DRlo/neg CD33+ CD14+ CD15+ granulocytic MDSC),
Neutrophils (SSChi CD11b+ CD14lo/neg HLA-DR- CD14+ CD15+ CD16hi CD11+)
Eosinophils (SSChi HLA-DR- CD15+ CD16-).

title: CB24. Disaggregation of human breast tumors
text:
Disaggregation of human breast tumors (CB 24)
NOTE:
After the breast tumor is surgically removed, it is placed in wash media: RPMI 1640 (Lonza) supplemented with 2% FBS (Sigma-Aldrich) and 1% Penicillin-Streptomycin (Euroclone) and brought immediately to the lab. Samples are processed within 60 minutes from removal.
Time:
1h and 30 minutes
Materials:

Petri dish
Scissors
100 μm Cell strainer
Sterile physiological saline solution (NaCl 0,9%. Baxter)/ 1X PBS /HBSS
Black rubber bottom of a 5 mL syringe
Falcons (50mL)
Trypan Blue 0,04%
Labelled Cryovials
Cryobox (RT)
Freezing Medium (FBS 10% DMSO 4°C)
Liberase TL Research Grade
DMEM
Scales

Protocol

Weigh and measure the tumor tissue
The tumor tissue is sliced into 1-2mm3 pieces by sterile microdissection by use of curved scissors
Enzimatic digestion is performed with Liberase TL Research Grade. Use DMEM 10 mL/gr tissue and add 0.25 U/mL Liberase
Incubate at 37°C for 30 minutes
The sample is passed through a 100 μm nylon cell strainer. Gentle pressure is applied with the black rubber bottom of a 5 mL syringe to any remaining partially digested tissue on the cell strainer which was then washed with few mL of sterile physiological saline solution. NB: typically, <5% of the tissue (consisting of mainly acellular-connective tissue) remained on the strainer at the end of this step.
The sample is washed with 25 mL of sterile physiological saline solution.
The suspension is centrifuged for 15 minutes at 300 g at room temperature, max acceleration (9), max brake (9).
The cells are washed in sterile physiological saline solution (5 ml) and then counted in Trypan Blue 0,04%.
The cell suspension is centrifuged for 10 minutes at 520 g at room temperature, max acceleration (9), max brake (9).
The supernatant is removed and the cells are suspended in FACS buffer for staining or in cold freezing medium (FBS 10% DMSO 4°C) to 1 mL/vial
Vials are kept for 24/48h in a cryobox at -80°C, then moved to liquid Nitrogen container.

PBMC Isolation from Buffy Coat plus cell count & freezing
Materials

Sterile physiological saline solution (NaCl 0,9%. Baxter)/ 1X PBS /HBSS

Falcons (50mL)

RPMI 10
Labelled Cryovials
Cryobox (RT)

Protocol per 45ml of blood

Prepare 3 X 50 mL Falcons with 17 mL of Ficoll solution, RT
Dilute whole blood 1:2 (e.g. 45 mL blood plus 45 mL physiological saline solution)
Stratify diluted blood upon 17ml ficoll layer
Centrifuge: 400G, 30’, max acceleration (9), min brake (0), RT
Collect PBMC ring within the interphase, transfer it in 3 new 50 mL Falcon and bring to 40 ml with Sterile physiological saline solution (NaCl 0,9%. Baxter)/ 1X PBS /HBS
Centrifuge: 1600 rpm, 10’, max acceleration (9), max brake (9), RT
Remove supernatant, keeping in Falcon about 5 mL of saline solution
Resuspend pellet in 40 mL Sterile physiological saline solution (NaCl 0,9%. Baxter)/ 1X PBS /HBSS

1st Platelets Removal

Centrifuge 900 rpm, 15’, max acceleration (9) max brake (9), RT
Remove all supernatant.

ACK for red blood cell lysis

Add 1 mL of ACK Lysing Buffer to the cell pellet and resuspend the pellet;
Pull the 3 falcons in one tube and add additional 2ml of ACK 1X solution (total 5ml of ACK 1X solution), resuspend well the cells;
Allow the blood sample plus ACK Lysing Buffer to incubate at room temperature for 5 minutes. Lysis of the red cells should be evident during this incubation.
At the end of incubation, top up to 40ml with saline solution and proceed with the 2nd Platelets removal step.

2nd Platelets Removal

Centrifuge 900 rpm, 15’, max acceleration (9) max brake (9), RT
Remove all supernatant;
Resuspend pellet in 50 mL Sterile physiological saline solution (NaCl 0,9%. Baxter)/ 1X PBS /HBSS. First dilute with 2ml of saline solution and resuspend the pellet in order to destroy cell clumps, than top up to 10ml and resuspend again very well the cells, finally top up to 50ml and resuspend again the cell. In this way the cells

Cell count

1st dilution 1:10 then dilute 1:5 (tot dilution 1:50) in Trypan Blue 0,04% (serial dilution 95uL Trypan Blue or Turk;



Centrifuge 1600 rpm, 15’, max acceleration (9), max brake (9), RT
Remove supernatant
Resuspend cells in culture medium according to the desired concentration

Or

Resuspend in cold freezing medium (FBS 10% DMSO 4°C) to 1 mL/vial
Keep vials for 24/48h in a cryobox at -80°C, then move to liquid Nitrogen container

title: CB46.Freeze PBMCs
text:
How to freeze PBMCs (CB46)
Materials:
Fetal Bovine Serum (FBS)
dimethylsulfoxide, DMSO
Labeled cryogenic vials
PBS-/-
Freeze Procedure:

title: CB46.Freeze PBMCs
text:
Freeze

Centrifuge cells in 50 mL Falcon tube at 520g for 10 minutes.
While cells are spinning, make freeze medium (e.g., 90% FBS, 10% DMSO, it should be used ICE COLD). Label cryogenic vials with date, cell type, and user’s initials.
Eliminate supernatant from centrifuged cells and add freeze medium. Resuspend cells carefully and rapidly.
Quickly aliquot 1 mL of freeze stock per cryogenic vial. Screw each vial closed.
Put vials into cryo-box and place box, into –80°C freezer.
After 24 hours, transfer the cryovials into appropriate rack in liquid N2 tank.

Protocol

title: CellTrace Violet
text:
Prepare CellTrace™ stock solution immediately prior to use by adding the appropriate volume of DMSO to one vial of CellTrace™ reagent and mixing well or use frozen stock
Pellet the cells by centrifugation and remove the supernatant.
Dilute the CellTrace™ DMSO stock solution in pre-warmed (37°C) phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) or other protein-free buffer to the desired working concentration (1–10 μM).






Note



I do 5 μM which is a 1:1000 dilution of the stock.


Gently resuspend the cells in the PBS dye solution.
Incubate the cells for 20 minutes at room temperature or 37°C, protected from light.






Note



Uniform cell labeling can also be improved by gently agitating cells during staining


Add at least five times the original staining volume of culture medium (containing at least 1% protein) to the cells and incubate for 5 minutes. This step removes any free dye remaining in the solution.
Pellet the cells by centrifugation and resuspend them in fresh, pre-warmed complete culture medium.
Incubate the cells for at least 10 minutes before analysis to allow the CellTrace™ reagent to undergo acetate hydrolysis.
Proceed with cell stimulation, incubation, or analysis.







Tip



Recommended concentration for CellTrace™ staining is 1–10 μM. A dye concentration of 5–10 μM is recommended for tracking five or more generations, while 1–2 μM may be sufficient for tracking less than five generations.

Spin

Incubate plate at 37’ C for desired amount of time

title: CD8 isolation and activation protocol
text:
CD8+ T Cell Enrichment from Spleen + Lymph Nodes
Nicole Scharping
Background:
This protocol is for the enrichment of CD8+ T cells collected from mouse spleen and lymph node tissues for activation and culture.
Caution:

CAUTION: Comply with all biological and chemical safety guidelines, including disinfection of all materials contacting cultures by autoclaving or by contact (15 minutes) with 70% ethanol or 10% household bleach.
All steps should be performed to preserve sterility in the Tissue Culture (TC) room in the biological safety cabinet using aseptic techniques
CD3 and CD28 Antibodies are kept in 4oC box in 4oC fridge in TC room
Biotin-Abs are kept in 4oC fridge in main lab area

What you need:

Biotin-Abs (see Table 1)
CD3 Abs
CD28 Abs
Phosphate buffered saline (PBS)
MACS buffer
T-Cell Media (R10)
Ammonium-Chloride-Potassium Lysing Buffer (ACK)
Miltenyi Streptavidin Microbeads
MACS column
Magnet for column
15 mL Falcon tubes

Procedure:

3 Hrs before plating: prepare 6-well plate with anti-CD3

Dilute CD3 Ab 5ug/ml in 1ml sterile PBS per well (coat 3 wells per 1 spleen+LN isolation)
Aliquot into a 6-well plate; tap plate to distribute liquid equally across bottom of wells
Incubate at 37oC for ~3 hrs

Process spleen and/or lymph node tissues collected from mouse

Homogenize tissue(s) in R10 with filter in a dish and place solution in 15 mL tube. Wash fixture with additional R10 to collect remaining cells.
Centrifuge at 1600 rpm for 4 min and discard supernatant
Resuspend pellet in 1 mL ACK and incubate at room temperature for 3 min
Dilute with 3 mL R10
Centrifuge at 1600 rpm for 4 min and discard supernatant

Treatment of cells with Biotin-Ab stain (see Table 1)

Resuspend pellet in 3ml Biotin-Ab stain in MACS buffer per spleen+LN
Incubate at 4oC (on ice) for 15 min
Add 10ml MACS buffer to wash
Centrifuge at 1600 rpm for 4 min and discard supernatant
Resuspend pellet with 500 uL MACS Buffer, then add 100 uL streptavidin microbeads
Incubate at 4oC for 15 min
Add 5ml MACS buffer
Centrifuge at 1600 rpm for 4 min and discard supernatant
Resuspend pellet in 1mL MACS buffer

Column purification of streptavidin-bound cells

Attach MACS column to magnet
Pre-treat MACS column with 3 mL MACS buffer and discard flow-through
Run cell solution through column, collecting flow-through
Wash column two times (2X) with 3 mL MACS buffer, collecting flow-through
Centrifuge at 1600 rpm for 4 min and discard supernatant
Resuspend pellet in 6ml R10
Count cells using Beckman Coulter Cell Counter and record
Add 2ug/ml CD28, 1:2000 IL2 (50U/mL)

Plating cells in pre-treated 6-well plate (see step 1)

Pipette off PBS/CD3 from plate, getting the plate dry (discard liquid)
Gently! plate 2mL solution per well (6mL goes into 3 wells total)
Incubate at 37oC for activation for 24hr

title: CD8 isolation and activation
text:
CD8 Isolation and Activation
Coat Plates for activation
For goat anti-hamster coated plates

Prepare Antibody-Coated Plate (Start 2+ hrs before plating)
Preparing a 1:30 dilution of Goat Anti-Hamster IgG antibody in sterile PBS.
Coat wells by adding 550 µL of the diluted GAH-IgG solution to each required well of a 6-well round-bottom plate.
Gently tap the plate to ensure the bottom of each well is fully coated.
Place the plate in a 37°C incubator for at least 2 hours (or overnight at 4°C).

Spleen/lymph node harvest and homogenization

Grab spleen and lymph nodes (inguinal, brachial, and axilliary, avoid mLN if you can) and put in a tube with R10
Prepare Single-Cell Suspension by washing spleen/lymph nodes over a 70 uM filter in a petri dish
When spleen in homogenized, place 70 um filter over 50 ml conical
Wash filter by washing the petri dish 2x with 1 ml of RP5
Wash cells 1x at 1600 RPM for 4 min
Dump and add 1 ml ACK lysis and incubate for 4 min
Add 40 ml MACS buffer and spin at 1600 RPM for 4 min
Prepare Biotinylated Antibody Cocktail. The volumes below are per sample (adjust as needed based on cell number, typically for up to  total cells).







Antibody Target






Cell Type Marked for Depletion






Example Volume










NK1.1






NK cells






3 µL








MHC Class II






APCs (B cells, Monos, DCs)






3 µL








CD4






Helper T cells






3 µL








B220 (CD45R)






B cells






3 µL








Ter119






Erythroid lineage cells

Ly-6G/Ly-6C (Gr-1)






Granulocytes (Neutrophils)






3 µL








MACS buffer








600 µL







Note: This cocktail targets major non-CD8+ T cell populations. Adjust cocktail based on specific experimental needs or available antibodies.

Negative Selection Staining & Bead Incubation

Resuspend the cell pellet in 500 µL of the freshly prepared Biotinylated Antibody Cocktail (adjust volume based on cell number if necessary, typically ~100 µL per 10^7 cells).
Incubate for 15 minutes at 4°C (in the fridge), protected from light.
Fill the tube with MACS buffer (~10-14 mL). Centrifuge at ~400 x g for 4 minutes. Discard the supernatant.
Resuspend the pellet in 500 µL MACS Buffer. Add 50 µL of streptavidin magnetic beads.
Incubate for 15 minutes at 4°C, protected from light.
Fill the tube with MACS buffer. Centrifuge at ~400 x g for 4 minutes. Discard the supernatant. During centrifuge step, wash MACS column (e.g. LS column) in the magnet by rinsing with 3 ml of MACS buffer. Discard flow through. Don’t let filter dry so add more if needed during centrifuge step.
Resuspend the pellet in 500 µL MACS buffer.





Magnetic Column Separation

Apply the cell suspension onto the column.
Collect the unlabeled cells that pass through the column. This fraction contains the enriched, untouched CD8+ T cells.
Wash the column three times (3x) with 3 mL of MACS buffer each time. Collect these washes and combine them with the initial flow-through.
Centrifuge the collected flow-through at 1600 RPM for 4 minutes. Discard the supernatant.
Resuspend the purified CD8+ T cell pellet in a small volume (e.g., 500 µL) of R10. Count the cells using a hemocytometer or automated counter. Determine cell viability (e.g., using Trypan Blue).
Stop here and check CD8 T cell purity by flow (pre and post isolation)

We had 89% purity post isolation of CD8 T cells and 44e6 cells total. Resuspend to 2e6 cells/ml. Plate 1 ml.

Run flow to check purity (can assume 90-95% if in a hurry but always better to flow check)
Stain aliquot of cells with FITC-CD8b (1:100)
Wash 1x with FACS and run on flow.






Cell Plating and Activation

Retrieve the GAH-IgG or anti-CD3 coated plate from the incubator. Carefully aspirate the coating solution from the wells.
Wash each well twice with 1 mL of R10 to remove any residual unbound antibody. Aspirate thoroughly after the final wash.
Dilute anti-CD3 and anti-CD28 antibodies each 1:500 in R10 for GAH-IgG coated wells. Dilute anti-CD28 for the anti-CD3 plate coated wells at 1:250 so there will be 1 ug/ml anti-CD28 in final well.
Add 1 ml of the CD8 T cell suspension (containing cells) to each prepared well.
Add 1 ml of the anti-CD3/CD28 antibody (or just anti-CD28) mixture to each well containing cells (total volume per well = 2 mL). Gently pipette up and down or swirl the plate to mix.

Final concentration: 1 x 106 cells/mL
Final antibody dilution: 1:1000 (effective concentration depends on stock)

Place the plate in a 37°C, 5% CO2 incubator for 18-24 hours.

title: TRM in vitro differentiation
text:
Method

Coat a flat bottom 6-well plate with anti-CD3 (1 μg/ml for TRM, 3µg/ml for control/effector T cells) in 1ml PBS per well, and place at 37°C for 3hr.
Per mouse, harvest the spleen and peripheral lymph nodes. Magnetically isolate CD8 T cells per lab protocol.
PBS is removed after 3hr and enriched CD8+ T cells are gently plated at a density of 5 million cells per well in complete RPMI (cRPMI - a media containing RPMI supplemented with 10% FCS, 2.5% 1M HEPES, 1% 200 mM L-glutamine, 1% PenStrep (10000 U/ml penicillin + 10000 μg/ml streptomycin) and 0.1% 5*10-2M β-mercaptoethanol) along with 2ug/ml anti-CD28 and 50U/ml IL2. I usually do 2ml media per well. Plates are incubated at 37°C in 5% CO2.
After 24hr, cells are taken off stimulation, washed with cRPMI, spin down, and replate either with 25U/ml IL2 for control/effector T cells or with TRM polarizing media: 25U/ml IL-2, 10ng/ml IL-15, 10ng/ml TGFβ and 10nM retinoic acid.
Cell media is doubled every 48hr with new cytokines added only for the volume of media added. Old media is not removed. A fresh working dilution of atRA is needed every time additional media is added since atRA is light sensitive.
Cells can be used/analyzed on day 7.




This polarization media induces features of SI TRM (CD103+CD69+) as shown by flow cytometry analysis of CD103, CD69, IL18R and CCR9 expression

text:
Th cell differentiation in vitro protocol
Antibodies and reagents
Media is RPMI 1640 (for Th1 and Th2) or IMDM (for Th17) supplemented with 10% FBS, 0.5% penicillin/streptomycin, 2 mM L-glutamine, 1 mM sodium pyruvate, 10 mM Hepes, non-essential amino acids and 50 μM β-Mercaptoethanol.
Mouse specific anti-CD3 (2C11), anti-CD28 (PV1) and anti-IFNγ (R4/GA2) antibodies were from Bio Express (West Lebanon, NH, USA). Human IL-2 was from NCI Biological Resources Branch (Frederick, MD, USA). Mouse IL-4, IL-12 and IL23 and mouse-specific anti-IL-4 (11B11) antibody were from eBioscience. Mouse IL-6 and human TGF-β1 were from R&D Systems.
Helper T cell (Th) differentiation
Coat a 24-well plate O/N @ 4 °C with 1 μg/ml anti-CD3 and 2 μg/ml anti-CD28 antibodies. This is Day -1!
Prior to use wash once with sterile PBS.
Naïve T cells were isolated from mouse spleens and lymph nodes using the CD4+CD62L+ MACS kit from Myltenyi Biotec (Bergisch Gladbach, Germany) and seeded into plates anti-CD3/anti-CD28 coated plates @ 106/ml in 2ml/well. This is Day 0!
Helper T cell differentiation was induced by the following reagents:
- for Th1 in complete RPMI:
IL-2 (100 u/ml),
IL-12 (10 ng/ml) and
anti-IL-4 antibody (10 μg/ml);
- for Th2 in complete RPMI:
IL-2 (100 u/ml),
IL-4 (10 ng/ml) and
anti-IFNγ antibody (10 μg/ml).
On Day 3, expand each well of Th2 into a well of a 6-well plate containing 2 more ml of fresh media with IL-2 (same as above). Pool 2 wells of Th1 into a well of a 6-well plate containing 2 more ml of fresh media with IL-2 (same as above).
Th1 and Th2 cells were analyzed on Day 5 or Day 7.
Th17 were grown in complete IMDM with IL-6 (20 ng/ml), IL-23 (10 ng/ml), TGF-β1 (0.3 ng/ml), anti-IL-4 antibody (10 μg/ml) and anti-IFNγ antibody (10 μg/ml).
Th17 cells were analyzed on Day 4 (no pooling or change of media necessary!).
Th cell analysis
Cells can be analyzed before re-stimulation (“naïve” Th1, 2 or 17 cells) or after re-stim – the re-stim can be done with either anti-CD3 (can be coated on a plate (preffered) or added in solution; no anti-CD28 is necessary at this step!) or with PMA (50 ng/ml) plus Ionomycin (1 μM), depending on which function is analyzed!
Typically, PMA/I stim is used if cells are analyzed for intracellular cytokines for FACS (5h @ 37 °C stim – add Brefeldin A for entire duration of stim! Follow intracellular cytokine FACS protocol afterwards!), and anti-CD3 stim is used for cytokine analysis by ELISA (24 h @ °C stim).

title: CD8 activation protocol
text:
CD8+ T Cell Enrichment from Spleen + Lymph Nodes
Prepared by Hannah Tsunemoto
Updated February 15, 2016
Background:
This protocol is for the enrichment of CD8+ T cells collected from mouse spleen and lymph node tissues for cell cultures in 96-well plates.
Caution:

CAUTION: Comply with all biological and chemical safety guidelines, including disinfection of all materials contacting cultures by autoclaving or by contact (15 minutes) with 70% ethanol or 10% household bleach.
All steps should be performed to preserve sterility in the Tissue Culture (TC) room in the biological safety cabinet using aseptic techniques
CD3 and CD28 Antibodies are kept in 4oC box in 4oC fridge in TC room
Biotin-Abs are kept in 4oC fridge in main lab area

What you need:

Biotin-Abs (see Table 1)
Goat Anti-Hamster IgG Abs (GAH-IgG)
CD3 Abs
CD28 Abs
Phosphate buffered saline (PBS)
MACS buffer
T-Cell Media (TCM)
Ammonium-Chloride-Potassium Lysing Buffer (ACK)
Streptavidin beads
MACS column
Magnet (located in Hedrick Lab)
Round-bottom 96-well plate
15 mL Falcon tubes

Procedure:

2Hrs before plating: prepare 96-well plate with GAH-IgG

Dilute GAH-IgG Ab 1:30 in sterile PBS
Aliquot 50 uL/well into a round-bottom 96-well plate; tap plate to distribute liquid equally across bottom of wells
Incubate at 37oC for 2 hrs

Process spleen and/or lymph node tissues collected from mouse

Homogenize tissue(s) in PBS with frosted glass slides and place solution in 15 mL tube
Centrifuge at 1600 rpm for 4 min and discard supernatant
Resuspend pellet in 1-2 mL ACK and incubate at room temperature for 5-6 min
Neutralize with 3-4 mL MACS
Centrifuge at 1600 rpm for 4 min and discard supernatant

Treatment of cells with Biotin-Ab stain (see Table 1)

Resuspend pellet in 500 uL Biotin-Ab stain
Incubate at 4oC (fridge) for 15 min protected from light
Fill tube with MACS buffer
Centrifuge at 1600 rpm for 4 min and discard supernatant
Resuspend pellet with 50 uL streptavidin-beads and 500 uL MACS Buffer
Incubate at 4oC for 15 min protected from light
Fill tube with MACS buffer
Centrifuge at 1600 rpm for 4 min and discard supernatant
Resuspend pellet in 500 uL MACS buffer

Column purification of streptavidin-bound cells

Attach MACS column to magnet
Pre-treat MACS column with 3 mL MACS buffer and discard flow-through
Run cell solution through column, collecting flow-through
Wash column three times (3X) with 3 mL MACS buffer
Centrifuge at 1600 rpm for 4 min and discard supernatant
Resuspend pellet in 500 uL TCM
Count cells (1:1000 dilution) using Beckman Coulter Cell Counter
Dilute cells to wanted concentration of 2x106 cells/mL

Plating cells in pre-treated 96-well plate (see step 1)

Wash GAH-Ab with 100-200 uL TCM twice (discard supernatant into cell bucket)
Plate 100 uL of 2x106 cell/mL solution [final conc. 2x105 cells/well]
Dilute CD3 and CD28 Abs 1:500 in TCM
Add 100 uL CD3/CD28 Ab mixture to each well, pipette to mix
Incubate at 37oC until further processing

title: PCA: get most important genes
text:
DESeq2 has a convenient function to plot a PCA. However, is does not include a nice interface the get the genes, that are most important for each PC. Hence I create a small helper function for that purpose.
The function can be used with any DESeqTransform object created by normTransform, vst or rlog and returns a list with the most important genes for each PC.
#' Function to get the driving genes for each Principal Component (PC)
#'
#' @param object a DESeqTransform object, with data in assay(x), produced for example by either rlog or 
#'               varianceStabilizingTransformation.
#' @param n_genes Number of genes to return for each PC. (Default 10)
#' @param ntop  number of top genes to use for principal components, selected by highest row variance
#'
#' @return A list with the top `n_genes` for each PC.
getPCAGenes <- function(object, n_genes = 10, ntop=500){
  # this is the same as for plotPCA in the DESeq2 Package.
  rv <- rowVars(assay(object))
  select <- order(rv, decreasing=TRUE)[seq_len(min(ntop, length(rv)))]
  pca <- prcomp(t(assay(object)[select,]))
  
  # instead of plotting, we will get the eigenvalues
  loadings <- as.data.frame(pca$rotation)
  
  # and calculate the percent contribution to each PC here.
  aload <- abs(loadings) ## save absolute values
  res <- sweep(aload, 2, colSums(aload), "/")
  
  # return a list with the top X genes for each PC
  lapply(res, function(x) {
    top <- order(x, decreasing=TRUE)[1:n_genes]
    genes <- rownames(res)[top]
    sprintf("%s (%.2f%%)", genes, x[top]*100)
    })  
}
You can now get the most important genes with getPCAGenes(vst(dds)).

# BiocManager is an excellent source for R packages used in bioinformatics

title: Introduction to DESeq2
text:
Install required packages
The first thing we need to do, is install all the required packages in R. You can do this by running the following commands in R.
#| message: false
# BiocManager is an excellent source for R packages used in bioinformatics
if (!requireNamespace("BiocManager", quietly = TRUE))
    install.packages("BiocManager")

# these are the packages that we are going to need.
list.of.packages <- c("ggplot2", "DESeq2", "readr", "readxl", "pheatmap",
                      "RColorBrewer", "EnhancedVolcano", "fgsea", "org.Mm.eg.db",
                      "AnnotationDbi", "gage", "dplyr", "ComplexHeatmap",
                      "patchwork", "GSVA", "limma", "magrittr", "purrr")

# check, which packages have not been installed so far
new.packages <- list.of.packages[!(list.of.packages %in% installed.packages()[,"Package"])]
# install the missing packages. If a package is not in Bioconductor, it will be installed from cran. this can take a while
if(length(new.packages)) BiocManager::install(new.packages)

# This library is for prettier tables in the markdown.
library(printr)

title: Introduction to DESeq2
section: Load count data and sample annotation into R
text:
Load count data and sample annotation into R
The next thing we need to do, is to load the raw count data and the sample annotation into R. We can import excel files with read_excel from the package readxl and the CSV file with read_csv from readr. First, we load the libraries in R, then we can access their function to load the data.
You can download the file here: GeneMatrix Annotation
#| label: tbl-counts_annotation
#| tbl-cap:
#|   - "Raw counts"
#|   - "Sample annotation"
#| message: false
library(readxl)
counts <- read_excel("GeneMatrix_all_Ms.xlsx")
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
annotation <- read_csv("annotation.csv")
## let's inspect the files
head(counts)
head(annotation)

Prepare counts data
As you can see, in this case the counts table has 11 columns. The first two have the gene names, the last 9 contain the actual counts that we are interested in. DESeq requires a table, that only contains the counts. The row names contain the information about the gene. So let’s do that.
#| label: tbl-counts
#| tbl-cap: "Prepare the counts table for DESeq"
# to set to rownames, we first have to convert the table to a data.frame
counts <- as.data.frame(counts)
# Set the column ENSMUSG as the rownames of the table.
rownames(counts) <- counts$Gene_ID_ENSMUSG
# Remove ENSMUSG and Gene_Id from the table
counts$Gene_ID_ENSMUSG <- NULL
counts$Gene_ID <- NULL

head(counts)
Now we have a table with the samples as columns and the gene as rows (See ?@tbl-counts).


Prepare annotation
Next, let’s have a look at the annotation file. For each column in counts, we need one row in the annotation file. In this case, the row name needs to be the sample name. Then we will do some checks. We want to make sure that we have an annotation for all samples in counts and that the order of the column in counts equals the order of the rows in annotation.
# set rownames
annotation <- as.data.frame(annotation)
rownames(annotation) <- annotation$sample

# check if all rownames in annotation correspond to a column in counts
all(rownames(annotation) %in% colnames(counts))  # --> this should return TRUE
# check if they are in the same order
# if this does not return TRUE, do not worry about that. We will sort the columns of counts accordingly.
all(rownames(annotation) == colnames(counts))
# reorder the columns of counts
counts <- counts[, rownames(annotation)]

# now, this sould return TRUE
all(rownames(annotation) == colnames(counts))

title: Introduction to DESeq2
text:
DESeq2
Here, we will use DESeq2 to analyze differential gene expression. DESeq2 has a very good vignette that explains a lot of the features of DESeq2. If you have any problem about running DESeq2 it is worth to check this page, as this provides a lot of answers: DESeq2 vignette

Create DESeqDataSet
With the count matrix, counts, and the sample information, annotation, we can construct a DESeqDataSet. The design formula depends on the experimental design of your experiment. In this case, tissue (Spleen, Fat, Gut) and cell.type (Trm, Tem). Let’s assume that there is no interaction between tissue and cell.type to make the analysis a little easier. Again, the DESeq2 vignette provides a very nice section on how to deal with interaction in DESeq2
#| message: false
#| warning: false
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(DESeq2))

dds <- DESeqDataSetFromMatrix(countData = counts,
                              colData = annotation,
                              design = ~ tissue + cell.type)
dds <- DESeq(dds)
dds
If you have additional feature data (gene data, eg. names), it can be added to the DESeqDataSet by adding to the metadata columns of a newly constructed object using the mcol function. Let us add the Gene_ID_ENSMUSG and Gene_ID.
#| label: tbl-gene_information
#| tbl-cap: "Gene information: Ensembl ID and gene name."
# read the excel file, but keep only the first to columns  [,1:2]
gene_information <- read_excel("GeneMatrix_all_Ms.xlsx")[,1:2]
head(gene_information)
mcols(dds) <- DataFrame(mcols(dds), gene_information)
# head(as.data.frame(mcols(dds)))

(Optional) Pre-filtering
While it is not necessary to pre-filter low count genes before running the DESeq2 functions, there are two reasons which make pre-filtering useful: by removing rows in which there are very few reads, we reduce the memory size of the dds data object, and we increase the speed of the transformation and testing functions within DESeq2. Here we perform a minimal pre-filtering to keep only rows that have at least 10 reads total.
keep <- rowSums(counts(dds)) >= 10
dds <- dds[keep,]



PCA
In order to check for batch effects etc. I find it useful to have a look at the PCA before starting with the DE analysis.
For downstream analyses – e.g. for visualization or clustering but NOT for DE analysis(!) – it might be useful to work with transformed versions of the count data. The most obvious choice for transformation is log transformation with a pseudocount. However, the DESeq2 package offers two alternative ways for data transformation (VST and rlog).
The be honest, I do not understand the mathematical background of either of these. But again there is a whole section on data transformation in the vignette.
Let us just do all normalizations and compare the results.
#| label: fig-pca
#| layout-ncol: 2
#| fig-cap: PCA
#| fig-subcap: 
#|   - "based on `normTransform`"
#|   - "based on `vst`"
#|   - "based on `rlog`"
ntd <- normTransform(dds)  ## log2(n +1)
vsd <- vst(dds, blind=FALSE)
rld <- rlog(dds, blind=FALSE)

plotPCA(ntd, intgroup=c("tissue", "cell.type")) + ggplot2::theme_bw()
plotPCA(vsd, intgroup=c("tissue", "cell.type")) + ggplot2::theme_bw()
plotPCA(rld, intgroup=c("tissue", "cell.type")) + ggplot2::theme_bw()
In all three cases (?@fig-pca), we get the biggest difference in the PCA between the tissues and the Tem and Trm in mAT seem to be closer together.

Sample to sample distance matrix
An alternative way is to visualize the sample to sample distance (?@fig-distance).
#| label: fig-distance
#| fig-cap: Sample to sample distance
library(pheatmap)
library(RColorBrewer)
sampleDists <- dist(t(assay(vsd)))
sampleDistMatrix <- as.matrix(sampleDists)
rownames(sampleDistMatrix) <- paste(vsd$tissue, vsd$cell.type, sep="-")
colnames(sampleDistMatrix) <- NULL
colors <- colorRampPalette( rev(brewer.pal(9, "Blues")) )(255)
pheatmap(sampleDistMatrix,
         clustering_distance_rows=sampleDists,
         clustering_distance_cols=sampleDists,
         col=colors)



Differential expression analysis
For the DE analysis, you first have to know which groups you want to compare. For some special comparisons you might need to adapt the design when creating the DDS (see above). In this example, we want to compare mAT-TEM vs mAT-TRM.
Therefore we need to slightly adapt the experimental design. So far we have ~ tissue + cell.type. If we were to compare Tem vs Trm in this design, the Tem population would consist of Spl and mAT and the Trm population of mAT and LP. We could either add an interaction term or create a new grouping variable by pasting tissue and cell.type together.
#| message: false
# create new grouping variable and convert it to a factor
dds$tissue_cell.type <- factor(paste(dds$tissue, dds$cell.type, sep="-"))
dds$tissue_cell.type
# update design
design(dds) <- ~ tissue_cell.type
design(dds)
The actual analysis only consists of two commands: DESeq and results.
#| message: false
dds <- DESeq(dds)
# we want to compare mAT-Trm against mAT-Tem
res <- results(dds, contrast = c("tissue_cell.type", "mAT-Trm", "mAT-Tem"))

MA Plot
Let’s inspect the results with a MA Plot (?@fig-ma_plot). Points will be colored if the adjusted p value is less than 0.1. Points which fall out of the window are plotted as open triangles pointing either up or down.
#| label: fig-ma_plot
#| fig-cap: "MA Plot: Mean expression vs fold change"
plotMA(res, ylim=c(-2,2))


Shrinkage of effect size
Shrinkage of effect size (LFC estimates) is useful for visualization and ranking of genes. You can do this by running
#| message: false
resLFC <- lfcShrink(dds, contrast = c("tissue_cell.type", "mAT-Trm", "mAT-Tem"), type="normal")
resLFC
It is more useful visualize the MA-plot for the shrunken log2 fold changes (?@fig-ma_plot_lfc), which remove the noise associated with log2 fold changes from low count genes without requiring arbitrary filtering thresholds.
#| label: fig-ma_plot_lfc
#| fig-cap: "MA Plot: Mean expression vs shrunken fold change"
plotMA(resLFC, ylim=c(-2,2))
As you can see, lfcShrink removes the noise associated with log2 fold changes from low count genes without requiring arbitrary filtering thresholds. P values are not affected by this.
plot(res$pvalue, resLFC$pvalue)


Volcano plot
With this, it is really easy to create a volcano plot.
#| label: fig-volcano
#| fig-cap: Volcano plot
#| message: false
library(EnhancedVolcano)
EnhancedVolcano(resLFC,
    lab = mcols(dds)$Gene_ID,
    x = 'log2FoldChange',
    y = 'padj', ## use pvalue for unadjusted p values
    pCutoff = 10e-4,
    title = "Volcano plot",
    subtitle = "Comparison mAT-Trm vs mAT-Tem")
You can see, that e.g. 4-1BB (Tnfrsf9) is upregulated in Trm.


Summary of the results
summary(resLFC)
103 genes are upregulated and 100 are down regulated.
It can also be useful to plot the counts of a gene across the different groups. Let’s plot the gene with the lowest p-value.
#| label: fig-basic_counts
#| fig-cap: Plot of normalized counts of the gene with the lowest p-value
plotCounts(dds, gene=which.min(resLFC$padj), intgroup="tissue_cell.type")
I don’t really know many (or any) of the ENSMUSG by heart. So let us add the gene symbols stored in mcols.
## important: add additonal columns before you change the order of the results!
resLFC$Gene_ID <- mcols(dds)$Gene_ID
head(resLFC)
Much better… Now sort the list by adjusted p-value.
resOrdered <- resLFC[order(resLFC$padj),]
head(resOrdered)
We can export the list to csv (or excel) to make manual inspection a little easier.
write_csv(as.data.frame(resOrdered), "de_mAT-Trm_vs_mAT-Tem.csv")



Heatmap
Using the normalized counts, we can easily create a Heatmap displaying the differentially regulated genes.
#| label: fig-heatmap_de_genes
#| fig-cap: Heatmap of DE genes
# we are using which here, as some pvalues are NA.
de_genes <- rownames(resLFC)[which(resLFC$padj<0.1)]

# extract count data and filter rows.
m <- assay(ntd)[de_genes,]  ## or rld (for rlog) or vsd (for vst)

# keep only the samples, that we compared.
m <- m[, dds$tissue_cell.type %in% c("mAT-Trm", "mAT-Tem")]

suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(ComplexHeatmap))

Heatmap(t(scale(t(m))),     # we want to normalize the counts per row. 
                            # scale() normalizes per column.
                            # therefore we first transponse the matrix, 
                            # then call scale and then transpose again.
        show_row_names = FALSE,
        column_split = 2,
        row_split = 2,
        name="z-score")

title: Introduction to DESeq2
text:
GSEA

Prepare ranked gene list
In order to do a GSEA analysis in R, we need to create a ranked gene list. Many tools use the signed -log10(pvalue) for ranking of the genes. As the pvalue is between 0 and 1, the -log10(pvalue) will be between 0 and Inf. We use the sign from the log2FC to seperate between up and down regulated genes.
# function for signal to noise
# see: https://www.gsea-msigdb.org/gsea/doc/GSEAUserGuideTEXT.htm#_Metrics_for_Ranking
signal2noise <- function(var1, var2, col_names, log_counts)
{
  col_names2 <- colnames(log_counts)[col_names==var2]
  col_names1 <- colnames(log_counts)[col_names==var1]

  library(dplyr)
  assay(log_counts) %>%
    as_tibble() %>%
    rowwise() %>%
    mutate(mean1 = mean(c_across(all_of(col_names1))),
           mean2 = mean(c_across(all_of(col_names2))),
           sd1 = sd(c_across(all_of(col_names1))),
           sd2 = sd(c_across(all_of(col_names2))),
           ) %>%
    mutate(sd1 = if_else(sd1 < .2 * abs(mean1), .2 * abs(mean1), sd1),
           sd2 = if_else(sd2 < .2 * abs(mean2), .2 * abs(mean2), sd2)) %>%
    mutate(rank = (mean1 - mean2) / (sd1 + sd2)) %>%
    pull(rank)
}
#rank <- -log10(res$padj) * sign(res$log2FoldChange)
rank <- res$stat
#rank <- signal2noise("mAT-Trm" ,"mAT-Tem", dds$tissue_cell.type, ntd)
names(rank) <- rownames(res)
head(rank)
summary(rank)
barplot(sort(rank, decreasing = T))
As you can see, a few genes do not have a p-value, which is mostly because these genes have to few counts. We can remove these.
rank <- rank[!is.na(rank)]
head(rank)
Most of the gene lists available (eg. KEGG) use the ENTREZ ID as gene identifiers. Therefore we must match the ENSEMBL IDs to the ENTREZ IDs. The package org.Mm.eg.db has all these information stored in it. We load the package and use AnnotationDbi to match the ENSEMBL IDs (keytype) to the ENTREZ IDs (column). For some ENSEMBL IDs there might be multiple or none ENTREZ IDs. If there are multiple matches, we will take the first (multiVals="first") .
#| message: false
library(org.Mm.eg.db)
entrez_ids <- AnnotationDbi::mapIds(org.Mm.eg.db,
                         keys=names(rank), 
                         column="ENTREZID",
                         keytype="ENSEMBL",
                         multiVals="first")
## for 1838 genes there is no matching ENTREZ ID
sum(is.na(entrez_ids))
names(rank) <- entrez_ids
head(rank)
Now, we are almost set to run the GSEA. We only need the gene lists, that we want to test for enrichment. There are multipe sources to get pathway gene lists. In this example, we will use the KEGG pathways.


Retrieve pathways
The gage package has a convenient function to download the KEGG pathways. Since we will only use one function of that package, we will not load it using library but intead diretly access the function with ::.
The function gage::kegg.gsets returns a list with five entires.
kg.sets: KEGG gene sets, a named list. Each element is a character vector of member gene IDs for a single KEGG pathway. The number of elements of this list is the total number of KEGG pathways defined for the specified species.
sigmet.idx: integer indice, which elements in kg.sets are signaling or metabolism pathways.
sig.idx: integer indice, which elements in kg.sets are signaling pathways.
met.idx: integer indice, which elements in kg.sets are metabolism pathways.
dise.idx: integer indice, which elements in kg.sets are disease pathways.
We can use sigmet.idx to subset the kg.sets to only retain pathways that are important for signaling and metabolism.
pathways_kegg <- gage::kegg.gsets(species = "mouse")
pathways_kegg <- pathways_kegg$kg.sets[pathways_kegg$sigmet.idx]
head(pathways_kegg, 2)
The pathways only contain a list of ENTREZ IDs. So it is acually pretty easy to create a gene list you self, that you can than test in other settings.


Run GSEA (fgsea)
Now we can finally run the GSEA. UsingmaxSize=500 we limit the maximal size (= number of genes in that pathway). This speeds up the calculation as the time increases exponentially (not so sure about that, but I guess it is exponentially) with the number of genes in the list.
Note, if you are using a “older” version on fgsea you might have to add nperm=5000 to set the number of permutations to do. In the most recent version of fgsea this is no longer needed.
#| warning: false
#| label: tbl-gsea_results
#| tbl-cap: Results of the GSEA analysis.

library(fgsea)

fgsea.res <- fgsea(pathways_kegg,
                   rank,
                   maxSize=500)
## inspect the results
head(fgsea.res[order(pval), -c("leadingEdge")])
In this example we do not get any significant results from the GSEA analysis. If there are ties in the preranked stats, the p-value might change form run to run a little.`
If you wanted to further inspect a gene set, you can create the “typical” GSEA plot (@gsea_enrichment) using:
#| label: fig-gsea_enrichment
#| fig-cap: GSEA enrichment plot for T cell receptor signaling pathway
plotEnrichment(pathways_kegg[["mmu04660 T cell receptor signaling pathway"]],
               rank) + ggplot2::ggtitle("T cell receptor signaling pathway",
                                        subtitle = "Comparison mAT-Trm vs mAT-Tem")
I admit, this is not really exciting in this case.


Heatmap
#| label: fig-heatmap_gsea
#| fig-cap: Heatmap for differential gene sets
#| message: false
genes <- pathways_kegg[["mmu04060 Cytokine-cytokine receptor interaction"]]
subsets <- c("mAT-Trm" ,"mAT-Tem")

ensemblids <- unlist(mapIds(org.Mm.eg.db,
                     keys=genes, 
                     column="ENSEMBL",
                     keytype="ENTREZID",
                     multiVals="list"))
mat <- assay(ntd[rownames(ntd) %in% ensemblids,dds$tissue_cell.type %in% subsets])
#scale 
mat <- t(scale(t(mat)))
mat <- mat[!is.nan(rowSums(mat)),]

Heatmap(mat, 
        row_labels = mapIds(org.Mm.eg.db,
                     keys=rownames(mat), 
                     column="SYMBOL",
                     keytype="ENSEMBL",
                     multiVals="first"),
        row_title = "mmu04060 Cytokine-cytokine receptor interactiony",
        name = "ntd"
        )

title: Introduction to DESeq2
text:
GSVA
See this introduction & explanation
Gene Set Variation analysis is a technique for characterising pathways or signature summaries from a gene expression dataset. GSVA builds on top of Gene Set Enrichment analysis where a set of genes is characterised between two condition groups defined in the sample. GSEA (Gene set enrichment analysis) works on how genes are behaving differently between the two groups defined.
What if I want to study my samples for the enrichment of a pathway without relying on phenotypic information. What if I want to ask, how is this pathway or gene signature behaving in this sample? Gene Set Variation analysis can help me out here!
First we need to get the values to run the GSVA with. You can either use the counts, that follow a Poission distribution or the normalized values (here rlog). These values have a Gaussian distribution. Again, we map the ENSEMBL gene name to the Entrez IDs.
#| message: false
m <- assay(rlog(dds, blind = F))
entrez_ids <- AnnotationDbi::mapIds(org.Mm.eg.db,
                         keys=rownames(m), 
                         column="ENTREZID",
                         keytype="ENSEMBL",
                         multiVals="first")
rownames(m) <- entrez_ids
Now we can run the GSVA using e.g. the KEGG pathways (as in section GSEA)
#| label: tbl-gsva
#| tbl-cap: "Results of the GSVA analysis"
library(GSVA)
res_gsva <- gsva(
  expr = m,
  gset.idx.list = pathways_kegg,
  kcdf = "Gaussian",
      # Poisson if count data, Gaussian if log transformed (=continouus) data
      # see above, in this case we use counts, not rlog
  verbose = FALSE
)
head(res_gsva)
We get a table with one value for every gene set for every sample. You can imagine these as kind of summerized expression values for the genes in the gene set.

Test which sets are differentially expressed
To test which pathways show differences between the samples, we can use the limma package to fit models one the results obtained form the GSVA.
#| label: tbl-top_gsva_pathways
#| tbl-cap: Top differentially regulated pathways
#| message: false
library(limma)
library(magrittr)

design <- model.matrix(~0+tissue_cell.type, data=colData(dds))
colnames(design) <- make.names(levels(dds$tissue_cell.type))

fit <- lmFit(res_gsva, design = design)

# define contrasts of interest
# here we create all possible contrasts
cont.matrix <- colnames(design) %>%
    utils::combn(., 2, simplify = FALSE) %>%
    purrr::map(~paste0(.[2], "-", .[1]))
cont.matrix <- makeContrasts(contrasts = cont.matrix,
                            levels=design)

# fit the contrasts to the model
fit <- contrasts.fit(fit, contrasts = cont.matrix)

fit <- eBayes(fit)

# topTable gives the overall significant genelists (F statistics)
topTable(fit)
# Multiple Testing Across Genes and Contrasts 
summary(res_limma <- decideTests(fit))
#| label: fig_gsva_upset
#| fig-cap: Upset plot for GSVA results
# make upsetplot
UpSet(make_comb_mat(abs(as.data.frame(res_limma))))
Only few pathways show significant differences between all the samples (F statistics). Let’s plot these in a Heatmap.
#| label: fig-gsva_heatmap
#| fig-cap: Heatmap for GSVA results
#| message: false
significant_pathways <- rownames(topTable(fit, p.value = 0.05, number = Inf))

Heatmap(res_gsva[significant_pathways,],
        name="gsva score")

title: Build cellranger reference with YFP
text: This script will create a mouse reference that includes YFP. The reference can be used to align single-cell RNA-Seq samples using cellranger. For a long explanation on how to build the mouse reference see the protocol on the 10x website.

title: Build cellranger reference with YFP
text:
Prepare mouse fasta and GTF
First we need to download the fasta and GTF file and set some metadata for the refernce genome.
# Set metadata
genome="mm10-YFP"
version="2020-A"


# Set up source and build directories
build="scratch/mm10-2020-A_build_YFP"
mkdir -p "$build"


# Download source files if they do not exist in reference_sources/ folder
source="scratch/reference_sources"
mkdir -p "$source"


fasta_url="http://ftp.ensembl.org/pub/release-98/fasta/mus_musculus/dna/Mus_musculus.GRCm38.dna.primary_assembly.fa.gz"
fasta_in="${source}/Mus_musculus.GRCm38.dna.primary_assembly.fa"
gtf_url="http://ftp.ebi.ac.uk/pub/databases/gencode/Gencode_mouse/release_M23/gencode.vM23.primary_assembly.annotation.gtf.gz"
gtf_in="${source}/gencode.vM23.primary_assembly.annotation.gtf"


if [ ! -f "$gtf_in" ]; then
    curl -sS "$gtf_url" | zcat > "$gtf_in"
fi
if [ ! -f "$fasta_in" ]; then
    curl -sS "$fasta_url" | zcat > "$fasta_in"
fi
# Modify sequence headers in the Ensembl FASTA to match the file
# "GRCm38.primary_assembly.genome.fa" from GENCODE. Unplaced and unlocalized
# sequences such as "GL456210.1" have the same names in both versions.
#
# Input FASTA:
#   >1 dna:chromosome chromosome:GRCm38:1:1:195471971:1 REF
#
# Output FASTA:
#   >chr1 1
fasta_modified="$build/$(basename "$fasta_in").modified"
# sed commands:
# 1. Replace metadata after space with original contig name, as in GENCODE
# 2. Add "chr" to names of autosomes and sex chromosomes
# 3. Handle the mitochrondrial chromosome
cat "$fasta_in" \
    | sed -E 's/^>(\S+).*/>\1 \1/' \
    | sed -E 's/^>([0-9]+|[XY]) />chr\1 /' \
    | sed -E 's/^>MT />chrM /' \
    > "$fasta_modified"
# Remove version suffix from transcript, gene, and exon IDs in order to match
# previous Cell Ranger reference packages
#
# Input GTF:
#     ... gene_id "ENSMUSG00000102693.1"; ...
# Output GTF:
#     ... gene_id "ENSMUSG00000102693"; gene_version "1"; ...
gtf_modified="$build/$(basename "$gtf_in").modified"
# Pattern matches Ensembl gene, transcript, and exon IDs for human or mouse:
ID="(ENS(MUS)?[GTE][0-9]+)\.([0-9]+)"
cat "$gtf_in" \
    | sed -E 's/gene_id "'"$ID"'";/gene_id "\1"; gene_version "\3";/' \
    | sed -E 's/transcript_id "'"$ID"'";/transcript_id "\1"; transcript_version "\3";/' \
    | sed -E 's/exon_id "'"$ID"'";/exon_id "\1"; exon_version "\3";/' \
    > "$gtf_modified"
# Define string patterns for GTF tags
# NOTES:
# - Since GENCODE release 31/M22 (Ensembl 97), the "lincRNA" and "antisense"
#   biotypes are part of a more generic "lncRNA" biotype.
# - These filters are relevant only to GTF files from GENCODE. The GTFs from
#   Ensembl release 98 have the following differences:
#   - The names "gene_biotype" and "transcript_biotype" are used instead of
#     "gene_type" and "transcript_type".
#   - Readthrough transcripts are present but are not marked with the
#     "readthrough_transcript" tag.
BIOTYPE_PATTERN=\
"(protein_coding|lncRNA|\
IG_C_gene|IG_D_gene|IG_J_gene|IG_LV_gene|IG_V_gene|\
IG_V_pseudogene|IG_J_pseudogene|IG_C_pseudogene|\
TR_C_gene|TR_D_gene|TR_J_gene|TR_V_gene|\
TR_V_pseudogene|TR_J_pseudogene)"
GENE_PATTERN="gene_type \"${BIOTYPE_PATTERN}\""
TX_PATTERN="transcript_type \"${BIOTYPE_PATTERN}\""
READTHROUGH_PATTERN="tag \"readthrough_transcript\""
# Construct the gene ID allowlist. We filter the list of all transcripts
# based on these criteria:
#   - allowable gene_type (biotype)
#   - allowable transcript_type (biotype)
#   - no "readthrough_transcript" tag
# We then collect the list of gene IDs that have at least one associated
# transcript passing the filters.
cat "$gtf_modified" \
    | awk '$3 == "transcript"' \
    | grep -E "$GENE_PATTERN" \
    | grep -E "$TX_PATTERN" \
    | grep -Ev "$READTHROUGH_PATTERN" \
    | sed -E 's/.*(gene_id "[^"]+").*/\1/' \
    | sort \
    | uniq \
    > "${build}/gene_allowlist"
# Filter the GTF file based on the gene allowlist
gtf_filtered="${build}/$(basename "$gtf_in").filtered"
# Copy header lines beginning with "#"
grep -E "^#" "$gtf_modified" > "$gtf_filtered"
# Filter to the gene allowlist
grep -Ff "${build}/gene_allowlist" "$gtf_modified" \
    >> "$gtf_filtered"

title: Build cellranger reference with YFP
text:
Add the YFP
Now, we can add our “custom” gene to the fasta and GTF file. I downloaded the YFP fasta from the internet. We can inspect it using the cat command.
cat YFP.fasta
>YFP||720|<html><body>Topaz YFP, an enhanced yellow variant of GFP.</body></html>|linear
ATGGTGAGCAAGGGCGAGGAGCTGTTCACCGGGGTGGTGCCCATCCTGGTCGAGCTGGACGGCGACGTAAACGGCCACAA
GTTCAGCGTGTCCGGCGAGGGCGAGGGCGATGCCACCTACGGCAAGCTGACCCTGAAGTTCATCTGCACCACCGGCAAGC
TGCCCGTGCCCTGGCCCACCCTCGTGACCACCTTCGGCTACGGCGTGCAGTGCTTCGCCCGCTACCCCGACCACATGCGC
CAGCACGACTTCTTCAAGTCCGCCATGCCCGAAGGCTACGTCCAGGAGCGCACCATCTTCTTCAAGGACGACGGCAACTA
CAAGACCCGCGCCGAGGTGAAGTTCGAGGGCGACACCCTGGTGAACCGCATCGAGCTGAAGGGCATCGACTTCAAGGAGG
ACGGCAACATCCTGGGGCACAAGCTGGAGTACAACTACAACAGCCACAACGTCTATATCATGGCCGACAAGCAGAAGAAC
GGCATCAAGGTGAACTTCAAGATCCGCCACAACATCGAGGACGGCAGCGTGCAGCTCGCCGACCACTACCAGCAGAACAC
CCCCATCGGCGACGGCCCCGTGCTGCTGCCCGACAACCACTACCTGAGCTACCAGTCCGCCCTGAGCAAAGACCCCAACG
AGAAGCGCGATCACATGGTCCTGCTGGAGTTCGTGACCGCCGCCGGGATCACTCTCGGCATGGACGAGCTGTACAAGTAA
There are special characters such as “|” and spaces in the header (all text after the >) of this FASTA sequence. These can be problematic for downstream applications. It can be helpful to change the header to be more informative and also to remove these characters. The following command opens the file and uses the stream editor (sed) function to search for a pattern (the original header), replace it with new text (YFP), then directs the output to a new output file, YFP.mod.fasta.
Also, you have to make sure, that the fasta file ends with an empty line. This is especially important if you are trying to add multiple genes to the reference (e.g. YFP and GFP). If the fasta file does not end with a new line, the >> command that we use later will create an output similar to ...ACAAGTA>eGFP.... This is of course not correct (>eGFP needs to be at the start of a new line) and will result in an error when trying to create the reference genome.
cat YFP.fasta | sed s/\>.*$/\>YFP/ > YFP.mod.fasta
cat YFP.mod.fasta
>YFP
ATGGTGAGCAAGGGCGAGGAGCTGTTCACCGGGGTGGTGCCCATCCTGGTCGAGCTGGACGGCGACGTAAACGGCCACAA
GTTCAGCGTGTCCGGCGAGGGCGAGGGCGATGCCACCTACGGCAAGCTGACCCTGAAGTTCATCTGCACCACCGGCAAGC
TGCCCGTGCCCTGGCCCACCCTCGTGACCACCTTCGGCTACGGCGTGCAGTGCTTCGCCCGCTACCCCGACCACATGCGC
CAGCACGACTTCTTCAAGTCCGCCATGCCCGAAGGCTACGTCCAGGAGCGCACCATCTTCTTCAAGGACGACGGCAACTA
CAAGACCCGCGCCGAGGTGAAGTTCGAGGGCGACACCCTGGTGAACCGCATCGAGCTGAAGGGCATCGACTTCAAGGAGG
ACGGCAACATCCTGGGGCACAAGCTGGAGTACAACTACAACAGCCACAACGTCTATATCATGGCCGACAAGCAGAAGAAC
GGCATCAAGGTGAACTTCAAGATCCGCCACAACATCGAGGACGGCAGCGTGCAGCTCGCCGACCACTACCAGCAGAACAC
CCCCATCGGCGACGGCCCCGTGCTGCTGCCCGACAACCACTACCTGAGCTACCAGTCCGCCCTGAGCAAAGACCCCAACG
AGAAGCGCGATCACATGGTCCTGCTGGAGTTCGTGACCGCCGCCGGGATCACTCTCGGCATGGACGAGCTGTACAAGTAA
To find the number of bases in this sequence, we will use the grep -v "^>" command to search all lines that don’t start with the > character, which removes line returns with tr -d "\n" so they aren’t counted, and then counts the number of characters with the command wc -c. Each command is sent to the next step with the pipe “|” command.
The results of this command shows there are 720 bases. This is important to know for the next step.
cat YFP.mod.fasta | grep -v "^>" | tr -d "\n" | wc -c
720
Now, make a custom GTF for GFP with the following command. This command uses the function echo -e (prints everything in quotes; the -e enables interpretation of the backslash, e.g. . Use o insert the tabs that separate the 9 columns of information required for GTF.
echo -e 'YFP\tunknown\texon\t1\t720\t.\t+\t.\tgene_id "YFP"; transcript_id "YFP"; gene_name "YFP"; gene_biotype "protein_coding";' > YFP.gtf
cat YFP.gtf
YFP unknown exon    1   720 .   +   .   gene_id "YFP"; transcript_id "YFP"; gene_name "YFP"; gene_biotype "protein_coding";
Next, add the YFP..mod.fasta to the end of the genome FASTA. But first, make a copy so that the original is unchanged. Then, append the YFP.mod.fasta to the end of the reference fasta file. The >> means append. Note: Do not use >, which overwrites the original file.
fasta_modified_yfp="$fasta_modified.yfp"

cp $fasta_modified $fasta_modified_yfp
cat YFP.mod.fasta >> $fasta_modified_yfp
To confirm that the GFP entry was added to the FASTA file, use the grep “>” command to search for lines with the > character:
grep ">" $fasta_modified_yfp
>chr1 1
>chr10 10
>chr11 11
>chr12 12
>chr13 13
>chr14 14
>chr15 15
>chr16 16
>chr17 17
>chr18 18
>chr19 19
>chr2 2
>chr3 3
>chr4 4
>chr5 5
>chr6 6
>chr7 7
>chr8 8
>chr9 9
>chrM MT
>chrX X
>chrY Y
>JH584299.1 JH584299.1
...
>GL456368.1 GL456368.1
>JH584292.1 JH584292.1
>JH584295.1 JH584295.1
>YFP
Now, we do the exact same thing for the GTF file. We copy the GTF to a new location and append the YFP GTF at the end. Finally, we use tail to see if it was added correctly.
gtf_filtered_yfp="$gtf_filtered.yfp"
cp $gtf_filtered $gtf_filtered_yfp
cat YFP.gtf >> $gtf_filtered_yfp
tail $gtf_filtered_yfp

# basic function to plot a table, color scale is set to 70 and 90 quantile
plotTableHeatmap <- function(x, y,
                             label_x,
                             label_y,
                             margin = NULL) {
  tbl <- table(x, y)
  subtitle <- dplyr::case_when(
                   is.null(margin) ~ "Percent of total",
                  !is.null(margin) && margin == 1 ~ "Percent of row",
                  !is.null(margin) && margin == 2 ~ "Percent of column"
                                                                                     )
  m <- prop.table(tbl, margin = margin)*100
  m <- as.matrix(m)
  tbl <- as.matrix(tbl)

  col_fun = circlize::colorRamp2(c(0,
                                 quantile(m, probs = c(70, 90)/100),
                                 100),
                               c("white","yellow","orange" ,"red"))
  Heatmap(m,
         name = subtitle,
         col = col_fun,
         column_title = label_y,
         row_title = label_x,
         cell_fun = function(j, i, x, y, width, height, fill) {
                grid.text(sprintf("%i \n %.1f%%", tbl[i,j],  m[i,j]), x, y, gp = gpar(fontsize = 10))
          },
         rect_gp = gpar(col= "grey80")
    )

} # end function

# needs to be converted to Human ensembl gene ids
# One could use uppercase, but it is cleaner to use Biomart
# here's a small helper function for that
convertMouseGeneList <- function(x){
  require(biomaRt)
  human = useMart("ensembl", dataset = "hsapiens_gene_ensembl")
  mouse = useMart("ensembl", dataset = "mmusculus_gene_ensembl")
  genesV2 = getLDS(attributes = c("mgi_symbol"), filters = "mgi_symbol", values = x , mart = mouse, attributesL = c("ensembl_gene_id"), martL = human, uniqueRows=T)
  humanx <- unique(genesV2[, 2])
  # Print the first 6 genes found to the screen
  print(head(humanx))
  return(humanx)
}

# workflow form https://bioconductor.org/books/release/OSCA/multi-sample-comparisons.html#creating-pseudo-bulk-samples
# But i do not remove the low abundance genes as this would filter out HIC1
DEGenesWithoutAbundanceFilter <- function(summed, subset, contrasts=c("LocationIntestine", "LocationRectum")) {
  current <- summed[,subset==summed$singleR_labels2]
    # Creating up a DGEList object for use in edgeR:
  library(edgeR)
  y <- DGEList(counts(current), samples=colData(current))
  y
  discarded <- current$ncells < 10
  y <- y[,!discarded]
  keep <- filterByExpr(y, group=current$Location)
  #y <- y[keep,]  # we loose HIC1 here
  
  y <- calcNormFactors(y)

  design <- model.matrix(~Patient_ID + Location, y$samples)
  y <- estimateDisp(y, design)
  fit <- glmQLFit(y, design, robust=TRUE)

  df <- data.frame(
        Symbol = rowData(summed)$Symbol,
        Ensembl = rownames(summed),
        Subset = subset
  )

  for(c in contrasts)
  {
        res <- glmQLFTest(fit, coef=c)
        df[[c]] <- as.data.frame(topTags(res, n=Inf, sort.by = "none"))$FDR
  }
  #res <- glmQLFTest(fit, coef=contrasts)
  #summary(decideTests(res))
  
  #df <- topTags(res, n=Inf)
  #df$Symbol <- rowData(summed)$Symbol
  df
}

                                                                                                                colData = colData(sce)),

# function to calc p values using limma
DEAucLimma <- function(summed, subset, contrasts = c("LocationIntestine", "LocationRectum")) {
  library(limma)
  current <- summed[,subset==summed$singleR_labels2]
  design <- model.matrix(~Patient_ID + Location, colData(current))
  #message(colnames(design))
    
  #plot(plotExpression(current, rownames(current), x="Location", exprs_values="counts"))
  
  df <- data.frame(
        GeneList = rownames(current) ,
        Subset = subset
  )
  for(c in contrasts)
  {
        fit <- lmFit(counts(current), design = design)
         fit <- contrasts.fit(fit, coefficients = c)
         fit <- eBayes(fit)
         tt <- topTable(fit, number=Inf, sort.by="none")
         df[[c]] <- as.data.frame(tt)$adj.P.Val
  }
  df
}

p <- p_hic1_pval / p_tgfb_pval / p_trm_pval & plot_layout(guides = "collect") & ggthemes::theme_few() & theme(legend.position = "none") &
          scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, .1)))

#  p

ggsave(filename = "tscc/plot_hic1_tgfb_trm_with_pvals.png",
       plot = p,
       width = 8,
       height = 12)






Figure 8: Final plot
crumbs: HIC1 and TRM score in human scRNA

section: Display a motifs table with motif logos
text:
Display a motifs table with motif logos
# helper functions (not yet integrated into pySCENIC):

from pyscenic.utils import load_motifs
import operator as op
from IPython.display import HTML, display

BASE_URL = "http://motifcollections.aertslab.org/v9/logos/"
COLUMN_NAME_LOGO = "MotifLogo"
COLUMN_NAME_MOTIF_ID = "MotifID"
COLUMN_NAME_TARGETS = "TargetGenes"

def display_logos(df: pd.DataFrame, top_target_genes: int = 3, base_url: str = BASE_URL):
    """
    :param df:
    :param base_url:
    """
    # Make sure the original dataframe is not altered.
    df = df.copy()
    
    # Add column with URLs to sequence logo.
    def create_url(motif_id):
        return '<img src="{}{}.png" style="max-height:124px;"></img>'.format(base_url, motif_id)
    df[("Enrichment", COLUMN_NAME_LOGO)] = list(map(create_url, df.index.get_level_values(COLUMN_NAME_MOTIF_ID)))
    
    # Truncate TargetGenes.
    def truncate(col_val):
        return sorted(col_val, key=op.itemgetter(1))[:top_target_genes]
    df[("Enrichment", COLUMN_NAME_TARGETS)] = list(map(truncate, df[("Enrichment", COLUMN_NAME_TARGETS)]))
    
    MAX_COL_WIDTH = pd.get_option('display.max_colwidth')
    pd.set_option('display.max_colwidth', 200)
    display(HTML(df.head().to_html(escape=False)))
    pd.set_option('display.max_colwidth', MAX_COL_WIDTH)
df_motifs = load_motifs('pySCENIC/motifs.csv')
selected_motifs = ['Hic1','Klf2','Etv3']
df_motifs_sel = df_motifs.iloc[ [ True if x in selected_motifs else False for x in df_motifs.index.get_level_values('TF') ] ,:]
display_logos( df_motifs_sel.sort_values([('Enrichment','NES')], ascending=False))
